row.basis: rescued people led by God
row.note: The commentary places manna and quail after Israel's rescue from an enemy; this song says YHWH redeemed and led that people, supplying the narrative transition into the wilderness provision.

row.basis: bread rained from heaven
row.note: The commentary's gift that comes down upon the rescued Israelites meets YHWH's promise to rain bread from heaven for them; the verse makes the descent and divine giver explicit.

row.basis: quail at evening
row.note: The commentary names quail among Israel's bestowed food; Exodus reports quail covering the camp in the evening, the same wilderness provision scene.

row.basis: quail brought by YHWH's wind
row.note: The commentary joins quail with a warning that wrath may descend; Numbers has YHWH bring quail to the camp immediately before its punitive outcome, preserving both food and danger in one scene.

row.basis: anger after the meat
row.note: The commentary's warning that transgression after provision brings wrath closely meets the account in which YHWH's anger flares against the people while the quail is still in their mouths.

row.basis: manna given in hunger
row.note: The commentary treats manna as divine provision joined to moral direction; Deuteronomy says God fed Israel manna in order to teach dependence on the divine word.

row.basis: Spirit's instruction and manna
row.note: The commentary couples food, forgiveness, and finding the way; Nehemiah's retrospective prayer says God gave a good spirit to instruct Israel and did not withhold manna or water.

row.basis: heavenly manna suited to every taste
row.note: The commentary draws the ni'ma family's softness and delight out of the manna scene; Wisdom retells that manna as heavenly food containing every pleasure and fitted to each taste.

row.basis: calf and turning aside from the way
row.note: The commentary makes the calf episode a junction of wrath and losing the way; Exodus says Israel quickly turned aside from the commanded way and made a calf.

row.basis: YHWH's burning anger at the calf
row.note: The commentary says calf worship incurs wrath from the Lord; YHWH tells Moses that his anger burns and proposes consuming the calf-making people.

row.basis: wrath against the people brought from Egypt
row.note: The commentary recalls a people rescued from an enemy who then risk wrath; Moses explicitly asks why YHWH's anger burns against the people brought out of Egypt.

row.basis: YHWH relents from disaster
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes descending wrath with abundant forgiveness; the calf narrative itself reports that YHWH relented from the disaster announced for the people.

row.basis: Moses angry on seeing the calf
row.note: The commentary says Moses returned to his people angry and grieving after the calf; Exodus narrates his anger blazing when he saw the calf and dancing.

row.basis: Moses fears anger and wrath
row.note: The commentary's calf scene holds wrath and a way back together; Moses says he feared the anger and wrath that would destroy Israel, yet YHWH listened to him.

row.basis: forgiving God, slow to anger
row.note: The commentary contrasts divine wrath with a forgiving end for those who return; Nehemiah interprets Israel's rebellion through God's readiness to forgive, grace, mercy, and slowness to anger.

row.basis: calf called Israel's god
row.note: The commentary names the calf as the concrete offense beneath the wrath; Nehemiah's liturgical retelling specifies Israel's making of the calf and its attribution of the exodus to it.

row.basis: merciful and gracious, slow to anger
row.note: The commentary opposes rida and ghadaab while retaining forgiveness after the calf; YHWH's self-proclamation names mercy, grace, patience, and steadfast love in that same aftermath.

row.basis: forgiveness and unremitted guilt
row.note: The commentary holds mercy beside real wrath rather than treating them as interchangeable; the continuation both forgives iniquity and says guilt is not simply cleared.

row.basis: favor, pardon, and inheritance
row.note: The commentary's favorable group receives grace and travels together; Moses asks that, if he has found favor, God pardon the people and take them as an inheritance.

row.basis: Thirteen Attributes after the calf
row.note: The commentary needs the relation of calf-wrath to forgiveness; this rabbinic reading makes Exodus 34's attributes a liturgical pattern by which Israel seeks pardon after sin.

row.basis: calf, sacrifice, and rejoicing
row.note: The commentary's calf episode is retold here with Israel making the calf, offering sacrifice to it, and rejoicing in what their hands made.

row.basis: all ate spiritual food
row.note: The commentary's wilderness food is recalled by Paul as the spiritual food shared by the whole exodus generation, a Christian rereading of the manna gift.

row.basis: God not pleased in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary makes divine pleasure the opposite of wrath; Paul says God was not pleased with most of the manna-fed generation and their bodies were scattered in the wilderness.

row.basis: warning from the calf episode
row.note: The commentary uses the calf to connect provision, idolatry, and wrath; Paul invokes the calf tradition to warn his readers not to be idolaters.

row.basis: anger and hearts always astray
row.note: The commentary binds divine anger to losing the right path; this wilderness interpretation says God was angry because the generation went astray in heart and did not know his ways.

row.basis: angry forty years and fallen bodies
row.note: The commentary calls wrath a fall; Hebrews explicitly asks whether God was angry with those whose bodies fell in the wilderness.

row.basis: Jesus as exodus deliverer and judge
row.note: The commentary recalls God delivering Israel and then judging rebellion; Jude's text names Jesus as the one who saved a people from Egypt and later destroyed unbelievers, a Christological retelling of the scene.

row.basis: wrath poured upon a collective
row.note: The commentary dwells on wrath descending upon alayhim; Zephaniah has YHWH say he will pour his indignation and burning anger upon them, making the agent and collective onset explicit.

row.basis: anger, perishing in the way, and blessing
row.note: The commentary makes wrath a loss of the way while the other group is favored; this verse joins divine anger, perishing in the way, and blessing for those who take refuge.

row.basis: anger set against favor
row.note: The commentary explicitly sets rida against ghadaab; the psalm compresses the same polarity into God's momentary anger and lifelong favor.

row.basis: no'am of God upon us
row.note: The commentary's n-' -m family joins bestowed favor to softness; Hebrew no'am, a cognate form, asks that God's pleasantness or favor be upon us, closely matching the favor-upon-a-group construction.

row.basis: anger and a fallen face
row.note: The commentary says anger leaves a visible face; after Cain's offering is not regarded, he becomes very angry and his face falls.

row.basis: favor brightening the eyes
row.note: The commentary gives favor a softened face and cooled eye; Ezra calls the remnant's reprieve divine favor and says it brightens their eyes and gives reviving.

row.basis: divine face shining with grace
row.note: The commentary's blessed side is visibly softened and bright; the priestly blessing asks that YHWH's face shine upon the people and be gracious to them.

row.basis: lifted face and peace
row.note: The commentary contrasts a burdened face with a favored one; the blessing asks YHWH to lift his face toward the people and give them peace.

row.basis: Moses' radiant face
row.note: The commentary makes favor legible in a brightened face; Moses' face radiates after speaking with YHWH, supplying a concrete biblical face-of-divine-encounter image.

row.basis: end-time life or contempt
row.note: The commentary describes the final day as two visibly different destinies; Daniel's resurrection vision divides the sleepers between everlasting life and everlasting contempt.

row.basis: the righteous shine
row.note: The commentary's favored faces are luminous; Daniel says the wise, including those who turn many to righteousness, will shine like the expanse and stars.

row.basis: anger and a person following his own way
row.note: The commentary links anger to straying from the path; Isaiah says God was angry at iniquity, yet the person went on in the way of his own heart.

row.basis: healing and guidance after waywardness
row.note: The commentary's alternative to wrath is forgiveness followed by finding the way; immediately after the angry-wandering image, God says he will heal, lead, and restore comfort.

row.basis: return and no perpetual anger
row.note: The commentary places repentance and forgiveness against wrath; the summons to faithless Israel to return grounds mercy in God's refusal to keep anger forever.

row.basis: return, mercy, and relenting from disaster
row.note: The commentary's forgiving end asks for turning back after wrongdoing; Joel calls for a return of heart because God is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and relents from calamity.

row.basis: God does not retain anger
row.note: The commentary sets divine anger against rida or merciful approval; Micah says God does not retain anger forever because he delights in steadfast love.

row.basis: turn from a way and live
row.note: The commentary says the forgiven turn toward the right way; God asks whether he delights in the wicked person's death rather than in that person's turning from the way and living.

row.basis: leave a wicked way and receive pardon
row.note: The commentary gives forgiveness a turn toward guidance; Isaiah calls the wicked to leave their way and return to YHWH, who will have compassion and abundantly pardon.

row.basis: blind led from darkness into a way
row.note: The commentary's opposing outcomes are found or lost way; YHWH promises to lead blind people by an unknown way and make darkness light before them.

row.basis: guided on a straight path without stumbling
row.note: The commentary's favorable group is a company on a road; Jeremiah's restored people are led by streams on a straight path where they do not stumble.

row.basis: bright path of the righteous
row.note: The commentary combines a favorable face with a rightly found path; Proverbs compares the righteous path to growing daylight.

row.basis: dark path and stumbling
row.note: The commentary connects loss of the way with the darkened other side; Proverbs says the wicked path is darkness and its walkers do not know what makes them stumble.

row.basis: known righteous way and perishing wicked way
row.note: The commentary's two groups are distinguished by the road they inhabit; the psalm contrasts YHWH's knowing of the righteous way with the wicked way's perishing.

row.basis: good eye, good companion, good way
row.note: The commentary reads the favored path as one walked with good companions and a settled eye; this mishnah deliberately pairs a good eye and good companion with a good way, then supplies their evil counterparts.

row.basis: wide way ending in destruction
row.note: The commentary's wrath side is a lost way and a fall; Jesus describes a broad way that leads to destruction and has many travelers.

row.basis: narrow way leading to life
row.note: The commentary's favored side is a found path; Jesus contrasts it with a narrow way that leads to life and is found by few.

row.basis: darkness overtakes a walker
row.note: The commentary says anger and error lose the road; Jesus says one walking in darkness does not know where one is going.

row.basis: darkness blinds the eyes and obscures the way
row.note: The commentary's hostile face includes disturbed eyes and its theological result is waylessness; this verse says hatred leaves a person in darkness, blinded in the eyes, ignorant of where to go.

row.basis: eyes opened, darkness turned to light, forgiveness
row.note: The commentary joins seeing, guidance, repentance, and favor; Paul's commission is to open eyes, turn people from darkness to light, and give forgiveness and an inheritance.

row.basis: light and feet guided into peace
row.note: The commentary puts the favorable face and the right road together; Zechariah's hymn says divine dawn shines on those in darkness and guides their feet into the way of peace.

row.basis: light of God's glory in Christ's face
row.note: The commentary makes divine favor visible on the face; Paul says God has shone in hearts to give the light of the knowledge of God's glory in the face of Christ.

row.basis: righteous shining at the consummation
row.note: The commentary's final-day favored faces shine; Jesus says the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom.

row.basis: Moses' face as fading glory
row.note: The commentary's bright face is set in a Moses-and-wrath complex; Paul rereads Moses' radiant face as the visible glory of the old covenant.

row.basis: unveiled faces transformed in glory
row.note: The commentary turns divine favor into a face's condition; Paul extends the Moses image to believers whose unveiled faces are being transformed into the same image.

row.basis: the Lord's eyes on righteous and face against evil
row.note: The commentary contrasts a favored group with those under divine disfavor and makes face and eye central; Peter juxtaposes the Lord's eyes upon the righteous with the Lord's face against evildoers.

row.basis: wrath has come upon them
row.note: The commentary emphasizes wrath as something that comes upon a group without naming its agent in the Arabic passive; Paul uses the closely parallel image that wrath has come upon them.

row.basis: day of wrath and righteous judgment
row.note: The commentary calls yawm the days carrying punishment and forgiveness; Paul speaks of a day of wrath and revelation of God's righteous judgment.

row.basis: eternal life for persevering good
row.note: The commentary's favor side includes faithful action and an ultimate outcome; Paul names eternal life for those persevering in good work and seeking glory, honor, and incorruptibility.

row.basis: wrath and anger for disobedience
row.note: The commentary makes wrath the adverse outcome of rebellion; Paul sets wrath and anger on those who reject truth and obey unrighteousness.

row.basis: children of wrath
row.note: The commentary ends with a collective named by wrath; Paul describes a former corporate condition as being children of wrath.

row.basis: mercy interrupting a wrath condition
row.note: The commentary does not end at wrath but gives forgiveness a path onward; Paul immediately counters the prior wrath condition with God's rich mercy and great love.

row.basis: appointed for salvation rather than wrath
row.note: The commentary divides humanity between a gift-bearing and a wrath-bearing outcome; Paul explicitly says God has not appointed believers for wrath but for obtaining salvation.

row.basis: blessed inherit the kingdom
row.note: The commentary's favored group receives a divine gift and shares a destination; the king calls the blessed to inherit the kingdom prepared for them.

row.basis: cursed depart to punishment
row.note: The commentary's second group bears divine wrath and abasement; the king's opposite verdict sends the cursed away to the prepared fire.

row.basis: company with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob
row.note: The commentary says the favored road is shared with exemplary companions; Jesus depicts many joining the patriarchs at the kingdom meal.

row.basis: outer darkness, weeping, and exclusion
row.note: The commentary gives the adverse group a dark, humiliated bodily condition; Jesus contrasts the kingdom meal with expulsion into outer darkness, weeping, and gnashing.

row.basis: hiding from the enthroned face and the Lamb's wrath
row.note: The commentary makes wrath and a face inseparable images; those facing judgment seek to hide from the face of the enthroned one and from the Lamb's wrath.

row.basis: great day of wrath
row.note: The commentary's yawm carries the two outcomes; Revelation calls the crisis the great day of their wrath and asks who can stand.

row.basis: servants see God's face
row.note: The commentary's favorable final side has a transformed face; Revelation's servants see God's face and bear his name on their foreheads.

row.basis: God's light on the final servants
row.note: The commentary's bright face belongs to a final favored community; Revelation says the Lord God will give light to his servants, with no more night.

row.basis: manna eaten yet death remained
row.note: The commentary presents manna as a remembered divine favor; Jesus contrasts that wilderness manna with death, so the Christian discourse assigns the old gift a deliberately limited result.

row.basis: living bread from heaven gives life
row.note: The commentary's descending provision is manna; Jesus identifies himself as the living bread come down from heaven, turning the exodus image toward his life-giving claim.

row.basis: all stray, iniquity laid on one
row.note: The commentary says a straying collective bears wrath upon itself; Isaiah describes all as going astray yet makes YHWH lay the iniquity of all upon a single servant, reversing the placement of consequence.

row.basis: Christ becoming a curse for others
row.note: The commentary contrasts a group under anger with a group granted favor; Paul presents Christ as becoming a curse in order to redeem others from the law's curse, a different distributive account of adverse judgment.

row.basis: servants fed and rejoicing while others hunger and are ashamed
row.note: The commentary's two groups receive contrary bodily conditions; Isaiah contrasts God's servants eating, drinking, and rejoicing with others' hunger, thirst, and shame.

row.basis: joyful heart versus pain and broken spirit
row.note: The commentary's favorable face is softened while the adverse face is afflicted; Isaiah continues the division with joyful song from the heart versus cry of pain and a broken spirit.

row.basis: faces to the ground in praise
row.note: The commentary depicts the favored, guided people prostrating and praises God; Israel sees divine glory and fire, bows with faces to the ground, worships, and gives thanks.

row.basis: communal bowing and praise
row.note: The commentary's selected group falls in prostration; at Ezra's blessing the people answer Amen, lift hands, and bow with faces to the ground.

row.basis: all heavenly attendants fall on their faces
row.note: The commentary joins the favored assembly to prostration; angels, elders, and living creatures fall before the throne on their faces and worship God.

row.basis: walking in light, fellowship, and cleansing
row.note: The commentary says the favored path is traveled with companions and ends in forgiveness; John links walking in light to fellowship with one another and cleansing from sin.

row.basis: manna distributed by moral standing
row.note: The commentary divides recipients of divine provision from those exposed to wrath; this rabbinic manna tradition differentiates where the righteous, intermediate, and wicked find the food, making provision a visible moral index.

row.basis: mercy overcoming divine anger
row.note: The commentary treats rida and anger as opposed divine dispositions; the high-priest tradition has God speak of mercy overcoming anger, an interpretive attempt to hold the opposition together.

row.basis: Hebrew alehem under poured anger
row.note: The commentary's grammar turns Arabic alayhim into the site of descending wrath; Hebrew alehem is its cognate prepositional form in Zephaniah's statement that indignation is poured upon them.

row.basis: Hebrew ratsah and accepted atonement
row.note: The commentary calls rida the opposite of anger; Hebrew ratsah, a likely cognate of Arabic rida, says the offering will be accepted for the worshiper to make atonement.

row.basis: no'am joined to ways of peace
row.note: The commentary associates the n-' -m family with a softened favorable condition and a path; Proverbs calls wisdom's ways ways of no'am, pleasantness, and all her paths peace.

row.basis: royal favor versus wrath toward shame
row.note: The commentary opposes favor and wrath and reads abasement in the adverse side; Proverbs gives the same pair in a king's favor for a prudent servant and wrath toward a shameful one.

row.basis: wrath like lion and favor like dew
row.note: The commentary contrasts an overwhelming anger with a gentle blessing that comes upon people; Proverbs compares a king's wrath to a lion's roar and his favor to dew on grass.

row.basis: light of a king's face and rainlike favor
row.note: The commentary's favorable face is soft and bright, and its blessing descends; Proverbs says life is in the light of a king's face and his favor is like a latter-rain cloud.

row.basis: faces as flames on the day of YHWH
row.note: The commentary describes anger in a reddened face and attaches outcomes to a day; Isaiah's day-of-YHWH terror says people's faces are flames, though the verse depicts fear rather than anger.

row.basis: Hebrew yom in a wrathful divine day
row.note: The commentary's yawm denotes days when punishment or mercy comes down; Hebrew yom is its clear cognate, and Isaiah calls the day of YHWH a day of wrath and fierce anger.

row.basis: dust on heads and faces lowered
row.note: The commentary has dust descend over adverse faces; Jerusalem's mourners put dust on their heads and lower their heads to the ground under judgment, a concrete adjacent image of abasement.

row.basis: faces blackened by disaster
row.note: The commentary contrasts luminous favored faces with a darkened other side; Lamentations says the sufferers' faces are blacker than soot.

row.basis: no more shame or pale face
row.note: The commentary's blessed outcome reverses the shame of adverse faces; the restoration promise says Jacob will no longer be ashamed and his face will no longer grow pale.

row.basis: seeing and becoming radiant
row.note: The commentary's favorable face becomes visibly bright; Isaiah says Zion will see and be radiant in the context of restored divine abundance.

row.basis: wisdom lighting and changing a hard face
row.note: The commentary says favor makes the face soft rather than frowning; Ecclesiastes says wisdom lights a person's face and changes its hardness.

row.basis: joyful heart making a face good
row.note: The commentary reads inner favor or anger through the face; Proverbs similarly says a joyful heart makes the face good while sorrow crushes the spirit.

row.basis: light of the eyes gladdening the heart
row.note: The commentary's ni'ma image is an eye made calm and refreshed; Proverbs links the light of the eyes with a glad heart and bodily renewal.

row.basis: favor sought and a no-longer-sad face
row.note: The commentary makes favor visible in a changed face; after Hannah asks to find favor and receives Eli's word of peace, she eats and her face is no longer as before.

row.basis: shame of face under sin and judgment
row.note: The commentary's adverse group bears a humiliated face; Daniel assigns shame of face to Israel and its rulers because of unfaithfulness before God's righteousness.

row.basis: tears wiped from every face
row.note: The commentary's final favorable face is relieved of its burden; Isaiah's salvation oracle promises to wipe tears from all faces and remove reproach.

row.basis: praise replacing a faint spirit and ashes
row.note: The commentary makes hamd the opposite of blame and favors a softened countenance; Isaiah's restoration gives a garland instead of ashes and a garment of praise instead of a faint spirit.

row.basis: curse for turning aside from the way
row.note: The commentary places divine disfavor upon those who lose the way; Deuteronomy defines the curse through disobedience and turning aside from the commanded way.

row.basis: life and good against death and evil
row.note: The commentary divides recipients into contrary divine outcomes; Moses sets life and death, blessing and curse before Israel and urges the choice of life.

row.basis: a holy way on which the unclean do not stray
row.note: The commentary's goal is a road not lost after forgiveness; Isaiah's holy way excludes the unclean and says even fools will not go astray on it.

row.basis: God teaching and leading in the way
row.note: The commentary describes hidaya as the counterpart to falling under wrath; YHWH identifies himself as the one who teaches for profit and leads in the way to go.

row.basis: walking all God's ways after the calf intercession
row.note: The commentary's mercy sequence ends in a rightly lived way; after the calf-and-intercession complex, Moses states the requirement to fear, love, serve, and walk in all God's ways.

row.basis: walking with God and turning many from iniquity
row.note: The commentary's gifted people travel a way together and turn toward guidance; Levi is said to have walked with God in peace and uprightness and to have turned many from iniquity.

row.basis: walking God's ways among those standing before him
row.note: The commentary calls the righteous a company on the favored road; the high priest is promised access among those standing before God if he walks in God's ways.

row.basis: falling on the face before covenant blessing
row.note: The commentary's chosen and blessed figures fall in prostration; Abram falls on his face immediately before God gives covenantal promises of fruitfulness and nations.

row.basis: faces down and confession after divine fire
row.note: The commentary associates prostration and praise with a divinely favored manifestation; after the fire, the people fall on their faces and confess that YHWH is God.

row.basis: tender mercy and dawn from on high
row.note: The commentary joins divine favor to the image of a day and light; Zechariah grounds the rising dawn in the tender mercy of God before its guidance imagery in the next verse.

row.basis: eyes of the heart enlightened for hope
row.note: The commentary makes the eye's condition carry guidance and favor; Paul prays for enlightened heart-eyes so believers know the hope of calling and inheritance.

row.basis: Jesus' face shining like the sun
row.note: The commentary gives the blessed face a luminous aspect; the transfiguration states that Jesus' face shone like the sun, within a scene of divine approval.

row.basis: Stephen's face like an angel's
row.note: The commentary treats the face as a bearer of a person's spiritual condition; Stephen's opponents see his face as that of an angel while he testifies before judgment.

row.basis: the healthy eye filling the body with light
row.note: The commentary's favorable eye is calm and bright; Jesus uses a healthy eye as the condition by which the whole body is full of light.

row.basis: bad eye and bodily darkness
row.note: The commentary's adverse face includes an afflicted eye and dark covering; Jesus's paired image makes the bad eye produce darkness throughout the body.

row.basis: blessed eyes that see
row.note: The commentary turns favor into an eye's state; Jesus calls the eyes blessed that see what prophets and kings desired to see.

row.basis: rescue from darkness into a kingdom
row.note: The commentary's divine deliverance moves people away from the lost side; Paul says the Father rescues people from the domain of darkness and transfers them to the Son's kingdom.

row.basis: praise from God at final judgment
row.note: The commentary opens its contrast with hamd, praise and approval, and names a day of reckoning; Paul locates each person's praise from God at the Lord's coming judgment.

row.basis: well-done approval and entry into joy
row.note: The commentary glosses hamd as approval or being pleased; the master praises the faithful servant and admits that servant into the master's joy.

row.basis: glory, honor, and peace for doing good
row.note: The commentary's favorable side receives an approving divine outcome; Paul promises glory, honor, and peace to everyone who works good, against the wrath named in the same argument.

row.basis: lost and found at a father's welcome
row.note: The commentary contrasts being lost with a forgiven return to the way; the father identifies the returned son as formerly lost and now found and celebrates him.

row.basis: repentance, turning, and erased sins
row.note: The commentary makes repentance and a turn toward right guidance the way out of wrath; Peter calls hearers to repent and turn so that sins may be wiped out.

row.basis: confession followed by forgiveness and cleansing
row.note: The commentary's grace side includes forgiveness after wrongdoing; John says confession is met by God's faithful forgiveness and cleansing from unrighteousness.

row.basis: no hunger, thirst, scorching, or heat
row.note: The commentary begins with wilderness food and ends with bodily marked destinies; Revelation's favorable multitude will neither hunger nor thirst and will not be struck by scorching heat.

row.basis: guided to living water and tears wiped
row.note: The commentary couples a gifted community with guidance and a relaxed face; the Lamb shepherds the multitude to springs of living water and God wipes every tear from their eyes.

row.basis: cloud of witnesses and a race to run
row.note: The commentary's favored way is a shared route with exemplary companions; Hebrews places believers within a cloud of witnesses and tells them to run the course set before them.

row.basis: glory's Spirit resting upon the reviled
row.note: The commentary's favor is something that descends upon a group; Peter calls reviled believers blessed because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon them.

row.basis: great grace upon them all
row.note: The commentary's en'amte alayhim has an explicit giver and a group upon whom favor rests; Acts says great grace was upon all the witness-bearing community.

row.basis: idolatrous mark on forehead
row.note: The commentary turns the calf's idolatry into a wrath-bearing fate visible on the face; Revelation marks beast-worshipers on forehead or hand before announcing their judgment.

row.basis: wrath drunk by the idolater
row.note: The commentary's golden-calf warning culminates in divine anger; Revelation gives beast worshipers wine of God's wrath, a later apocalyptic pairing of idolatry and wrath.

row.basis: dishonor transformed into glory
row.note: The commentary's two faces foreshadow differing final bodily states; Paul contrasts a body sown in dishonor and weakness with one raised in glory and power.

row.basis: lowly body transformed to glory
row.note: The commentary makes final grace visible in bodily appearance; Paul expects Christ to transform the lowly body into conformity with his glorious body.

row.basis: elders fall and worship in praise
row.note: The commentary's chosen company prostrates in praise; the elders fall before the enthroned one, worship, and cast down their crowns.

row.basis: hidden manna for the conqueror
row.note: The commentary recalls manna as an indicator of divine favor; Revelation promises hidden manna specifically to the one who conquers, relocating wilderness provision into an eschatological reward.

row.basis: Hebrew nehmad as desirable
row.note: The commentary glosses hamd as approving or finding something good; Hebrew h-m-d is plausibly cognate but in this verse calls the forbidden tree desirable to the eyes, so the semantic divergence rather than a direct parallel is the point.

row.basis: red face and shadowed eyelids in suffering
row.note: The commentary describes redness and the eye-area as outward marks of anger; Job instead describes his own face reddened by weeping and shadow on his eyelids, a specific but affectively different bodily image.

row.basis: manna explicitly called YHWH's bread-gift
row.note: The commentary's descent of ni'ma after rescue is named here by the Israelites as bread that YHWH has given them to eat; it supplies the explicit attribution absent from the passive wrath phrase.

row.basis: manna given for eventual good
row.note: The commentary combines wilderness provision with moral testing and a beneficial end; Deuteronomy says YHWH fed Israel manna to humble and test them, in order to do them good in the end.

row.basis: cloud and fire leading the people
row.note: The commentary's favorable alternative to wrath is a guided road; Nehemiah's retelling says God's mercies did not forsake Israel and that cloud and fire continued to lead them on the way.

row.basis: finding favor in God's eyes
row.note: The commentary glosses hamd through approval and turns ni'ma into favor bestowed on people; YHWH tells Moses that he has found favor in his eyes and is known by name.

row.basis: Moses bows in response to mercy
row.note: The commentary joins the favored, guided community with prostration; directly after the mercy-and-forgiveness proclamation Moses hurriedly bows his head to the earth and worships.

row.basis: plague after the calf
row.note: The commentary's calf-makers receive divine anger and abasement; Exodus closes the narrative with YHWH striking the people with a plague because of the calf.

row.basis: anger, hidden face, and people consumed
row.note: The commentary makes wrath a condition borne by a group and visualizes face; Moses says YHWH's anger will burn, his face will be hidden, and the people will be consumed by evils.

row.basis: lifted countenance versus sin at the door
row.note: The commentary's angry face is the inverse of divine approval; God's reply to Cain contrasts the lifting granted for doing well with sin crouching at the door if he does not.

row.basis: God's face set against the disobedient
row.note: The commentary pairs adverse divine judgment with face imagery; YHWH says he will set his face against Israel, after which they are defeated and flee.

row.basis: anger turned away into comfort
row.note: The commentary's central contrast is wrath against a merciful favorable state; this thanksgiving says God's anger was directed at the speaker but turned away, and God became comfort.

row.basis: face hidden in wrath, everlasting compassion after it
row.note: The commentary treats anger as a visible, descending judgment and favor as its contrary; Isaiah says God hid his face in overflowing wrath for a moment but has everlasting compassion.

row.basis: looking to God, radiant faces, no shame
row.note: The commentary's favorable final face is luminous rather than humiliated; the psalm says those who look to YHWH are radiant and their faces are not ashamed.

row.basis: face shining brings salvation
row.note: The commentary connects divine favor, a shining face, and deliverance; the refrain asks God to restore the people, make his face shine, and save them.

row.basis: no shame and a consequent fall
row.note: The commentary makes the adverse face abased and says wrath is a fall; Jeremiah says the wicked neither feel shame nor know how to blush, therefore they will fall.

row.basis: shame on every face in judgment
row.note: The commentary's final adverse side bears a darkened or humiliated face; Ezekiel's judgment scene says shame will be on every face as people put on sackcloth and tremble.

row.basis: joy for the faithful and shame for opponents
row.note: The commentary separates a favored community from an abased one; Isaiah tells those who tremble at God's word that God will appear to their joy while their hostile brethren are put to shame.

row.basis: rejoicing heart and flourishing body versus indignation
row.note: The commentary makes the two divine outcomes bodily visible; Isaiah promises servants a rejoicing heart and flourishing bones while God's indignation is known against enemies.

row.basis: good person obtains favor, schemer condemned
row.note: The commentary relates approval and praise to the contrary of wrath; Proverbs says a good person obtains favor from YHWH while a person of schemes is condemned.

row.basis: confessing and forsaking sins obtains mercy
row.note: The commentary's route out of wrath includes repentance and changed conduct; Proverbs contrasts hiding transgressions with confessing and forsaking them in order to receive mercy.

row.basis: grace and mercy upon the elect
row.note: The commentary's en'amte alayhim makes grace a gift resting upon a chosen group; Wisdom says grace and mercy are upon God's holy ones and care attends the elect.

row.basis: two spirits and their paths
row.note: The commentary's two groups have opposed paths, visual states, and ends; the Community Rule's two-spirits instruction systematically assigns light and darkness, conduct, and judgment to opposed lots.

row.basis: Way of Life and Way of Death
row.note: The commentary's road splits between a favored and a ruined group; this early Christian teaching opens with two ways, one of life and one of death.

row.basis: way of light and way of darkness
row.note: The commentary's found path is associated with brightness and its lost path with dark affliction; Barnabas frames its ethical teaching as the two ways of light and darkness.

row.basis: walking in day without stumbling
row.note: The commentary joins correct guidance to light and an unfallen walk; Jesus says that a person walking in the day does not stumble because that person sees the world's light.

row.basis: walking at night and stumbling
row.note: The commentary's wrath-side loses the way and falls; Jesus's paired saying makes the night-walker stumble because light is not in that person.

row.basis: darkness falling on a judgment-blinded eye
row.note: The commentary gives anger a bodily eye-image and says something comes upon its recipient; Paul announces the Lord's hand against Elymas, after which mist and darkness immediately fall on him and he seeks a guide.

row.basis: rescue from coming wrath
row.note: The commentary juxtaposes wrath with a saving, favorable end; Paul describes Jesus as the one who rescues believers from the wrath that is coming.

row.basis: chosen people called from darkness to light
row.note: The commentary's favored community is both chosen and visibly luminous; Peter calls a chosen people out of darkness into God's marvelous light.

row.basis: formerly without mercy, now receiving mercy
row.note: The commentary's two groups are distinguished by bestowed ni'ma versus divine disfavor; Peter contrasts being not a people and without mercy with becoming God's people and receiving mercy.

row.basis: conqueror inherits and belongs to God
row.note: The commentary's favorable side receives a gift and shares a divine companionship; Revelation promises inheritance and a God-child relation to the one who conquers.

row.basis: lake of fire for the unfaithful
row.note: The commentary's adverse group has an eschatological judgment distinct from the favored group; Revelation supplies the opposed fate for the cowardly, faithless, and idolaters.

row.basis: manna's honey-like taste
row.note: The commentary develops ni'ma as softness, delicacy, and a restful sensory condition; Exodus describes manna as white and tasting like wafers made with honey.

row.basis: manna before the people's eyes
row.note: The commentary gives ni'ma an eye-image while recalling manna; the dissatisfied wilderness people say that nothing is before their eyes except manna, an intentionally contrary eye-and-provision scene.

row.basis: God does not destroy after Moses' intercession
row.note: The commentary's wrath sequence is countered by forgiveness and a continued path; Deuteronomy's retrospective account says YHWH listened to Moses and was unwilling to destroy Israel after the calf.

row.basis: Moses offers himself for the people's sin
row.note: The commentary describes wrath as falling on the culpable group; Moses instead offers to be blotted from God's book if Israel cannot be forgiven, a different placement of the consequence within the same calf scene.

row.basis: forty-year provision without lack
row.note: The commentary's ni'ma is an enduring divine favor rather than a single meal; Nehemiah says Israel lacked nothing for forty years, with garments and feet preserved in the wilderness.

row.basis: shame prevents lifting the face
row.note: The commentary's adverse outcome is a humiliated face under sin; Ezra confesses being ashamed and unable to lift his face to God because Israel's iniquities have risen high.

row.basis: weeping and face-down confession
row.note: The commentary's guided, forgiven figures prostrate themselves; Ezra's confession is made while weeping and lying face down before God's house, gathering a repentant community.

row.basis: faces growing pale before the divine day
row.note: The commentary describes an anger-marked red face and a final day; Joel's approaching day makes the nations writhe and all faces gather pallor, a related but distinct facial response.

row.basis: judgment changing a king's facial color
row.note: The commentary reads judgment in the body's face; after the divine writing appears, Belshazzar's facial color changes and his body is visibly shaken.

row.basis: life and favor for finding wisdom
row.note: The commentary's blessing is joined to finding the right way; Proverbs says whoever finds wisdom finds life and obtains favor from YHWH.

row.basis: good understanding gives favor, treacherous way is hard
row.note: The commentary sets favor against the condition of the lost way; Proverbs joins good understanding that gives favor to the hard way of the treacherous.

row.basis: blessing God for evil as for good
row.note: The commentary begins with hamd and its opposition to blame while contrasting ni'ma and wrath; this mishnah requires blessing God for adverse events as for good, changing how praise relates to an unwelcome divine event.

row.basis: quick anger and difficult appeasement
row.note: The commentary treats anger and rida as opposed dispositions; this temperament teaching distinguishes people by being easy or hard to anger and easy or hard to appease.

row.basis: rejoicing with the persecuted prophets
row.note: The commentary enumerates prophets and martyrs among the favored companions; Jesus tells the persecuted to rejoice because their reward is great and the prophets were persecuted before them.

row.basis: judgment as loving darkness rather than light
row.note: The commentary's two groups end in luminous or darkened conditions; Jesus explains judgment through the light's arrival and evildoers' love of darkness.

row.basis: doing truth and coming to light
row.note: The commentary's favorable side joins right action to a found way; the one doing truth comes to the light so deeds can be seen as done in God.

row.basis: disfigured faces seeking human notice
row.note: The commentary makes a face show an inward religious condition and begins with praise; Jesus criticizes fasters who disfigure their faces to be seen by people, distinguishing their received human reward from divine regard.

row.basis: anointed head and washed face before the Father
row.note: The commentary's favorable face is not merely a legal verdict; Jesus tells secret fasters to anoint the head and wash the face so the Father, rather than observers, sees and rewards.

row.basis: wrath revealed from heaven
row.note: The commentary calls wrath something that descends upon people; Paul describes God's wrath as being revealed from heaven against ungodliness and unrighteousness.

row.basis: justification and rescue from wrath through Christ
row.note: The commentary describes repentance, faith, good action, and guidance as the route beyond wrath; Paul frames rescue from wrath through Christ's blood, a distinct Christian account of the saving transition.

row.basis: God's kindness and severity
row.note: The commentary's rida-ghadaab contrast is expressed as two divine dispositions; Paul asks readers to consider God's kindness and severity, with continuance in kindness opposed to being cut off.

row.basis: formerly darkness, now light, therefore walk
row.note: The commentary's contrast joins identity, light, and a road; Paul says believers were darkness but are now light in the Lord and commands them to walk as children of light.

row.basis: Christ shining on one who rises
row.note: The commentary's eschatological face is lit after a fall or deathlike state; the cited hymn commands the sleeper to rise from the dead so Christ will shine upon that person.

row.basis: patience seeking repentance rather than perishing
row.note: The commentary contrasts a wrathful fall with repentance and a found way; Peter explains divine patience as not wishing people to perish but to come to repentance.

row.basis: eye salve, white garments, and exposed shame
row.note: The commentary's two faces include afflicted eyes and visible favor; the risen Christ counsels the blind, naked church to obtain eye salve for sight and white garments to cover shame.

row.basis: God's glory as the city's light
row.note: The commentary's blessed final side is luminous; Revelation says the eschatological city needs neither sun nor moon because God's glory gives it light.
